name: Itbayat
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Yamada, Yukihiro. 2014. A grammar of the Itbayat language of the Philippines (also Yamada 2002 Itbayat-English dictionary); not found online

new_statements.quote: Stress is believed to be a significant feature in these dialects. For the vast majority of words stress falls on the last syllable and it is convenient and adequate if such words receive no accent mark. For the remaining words, stress on non-final syllables should be indicated by means of an acute accent mark ´. tiban 'look' / tsíban 'accompany'; mangamong 'taking fish from net' / mangámong 'general term for fishing'; takey 'field' / mákey 'like'; dekey 'small'.
new_statements.citation: Cottle, Morris & Shirley Cottle. 1958. The significant sounds of Ivatan. In Alan Healey (ed.), Studies in Philippine Linguistics (Oceania Linguistic Monographs 3), 24-33. Sydney: University of Sydney.
new_statements.locator: Section 4.5 Stress, p. 32 (dialect coverage stated p. 24: (a) Itbayat, (b) Northern Ivatan, (c) Southern Ivatan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. Opened (page image) and the extracted text layer of 10 pp. = pp. 25-33 + cover). Section 4.5 Stress on p. 32 reads exactly as quoted: "Stress is believed to be a significant feature in these dialects. For the vast majority of words stress falls on the last syllable and it is convenient and adequate if such words receive no accent mark. For the remaining words, stress on non-final syllables should be indicated by means of an acute accent mark ´." followed by the two-column table tiban 'look' / tsíban 'accompany'; mangamong 'taking fish from net' / mangámong 'general term for fishing'; takey 'field' / mákey 'like'; dekey 'small'. The reader only linearised the table with slashes;…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable in the great majority of words; a minority of words carry lexically fixed non-final (penultimate) stress, which is contrastive (minimal pairs) and must be marked. Itbayat-specific corroboration: Yamada 1972: 61 speaks of 'a two-syllable word with a stress on the last syllable' (pagad, koyis, parek), and Yamada 2002: 18 shows stress shifted to the initial syllable as a superlative suprafix (maavij 'beautiful' vs máavij 'most beautiful'). Moriguchi 1987 adds that Itbayat, unlike Ivatan, has no contrastive penultimate-length accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: A minority of words with non-final stress, contrastive with final-stressed homographs (tiban/tsíban, mangamong/mangámong, takey/mákey); morphological stress shift for the superlative (Yamada 2002: 18). Vowel length (VV) and consonant length (CC) are separately contrastive (Cottle 1958: 32; Yamada 2002: 6).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a phonemic/orthographic sketch (1958, SIL). The statement is pooled over three 'dialects' (Itbayat, Northern Ivatan, Southern Ivatan); no Itbayat-only statement of default stress position was found in the Itbayat-specific sources opened (Yamada 1972, 2002; Moriguchi 1987), which are consistent with it but do not state a general rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted rule (Cottle & Cottle 1958: 32) is stated jointly for three 'dialects' of Ivatan as then conceived: Itbayat (= ivat1242), Northern/Basco Ivatan and Southern Ivatan (both under Glottolog ibat1238); Itbayat is explicitly included (p. 24) but the sentence is not Itbayat-only. The Itbayat-specific sources opened (Yamada 1972 Gengo Kenkyu 61: 61; Yamada 2002 ELPR A3-006: 18; Moriguchi 1987 JAAS 33: 112, 114) are consistent with final default stress and add that Itbayat, unlike Ivatan, lacks a contrastive penultimate-length accent. Note the earlier world scan named Yamada 2014 as unreachable; Yamada 2002 (the ELPR dictionary with grammatical sketch) is in fact open on the TUFS repository, but its phonology section is silent on stress placement.

sources.note: Sec. 4.5 Stress, p. 32: stress is a significant feature in 'these dialects' (Itbayat, Northern Ivatan, Southern Ivatan per p. 24); for the vast majority of words stress falls on the last syllable (unmarked); a minority have non-final stress marked with an acute accent, with contrastive pairs tiban 'look' / tiban 'accompany', mangamong / mangamong, takey / makey.

sources.citation: Moriguchi, Tsunekazu (森口恒一). 1987. バタニック諸語（フィリピン）におけるアクセントの消失と発生 [Accent evanescence and genesis in the Batanic language group in the Philippines]. Journal of Asian and African Studies (アジア・アフリカ言語文化研究) 33: 107-125.
sources.note: Instrumental/comparative accent study of Batanic. English abstract p. 107: 'Itbayat and Yami do not possess the system, Ivatan and Babuyan Claro, on the other hand, do.' p. 112 table: Itbayat 語 × (no accent system), where 'accent' is defined as 'この場合のアクセントとは、すべて語末から二番目の音節 (Penultimate) の長短によって示される長さアクセントである' (a length accent on the penultimate syllable). p. 114: 'Itbayat 語と Yami 語の Iraralay 方言では確実にアクセント体系が存在しない' (in Itbayat and Yami-Iraralay an accent system definitely does not exist). Itbayat keeps /h/ where Ivatan lost it with compensatory penult length (mahata vs Ivatan ma:ta). Says nothin…

sources.citation: Yamada, Yukihiro. 1972. Consonantism in Itbayaten. Gengo Kenkyu (Journal of the Linguistic Society of Japan) 61: 57-82.
sources.note: Consonant-focused phonology; no stress section. p. 61 §1.2: 'An intervocalic consonant C2 in a two-syllable word with a stress on the last syllable [C1VC2VC3] tends to be a little longer than a single consonant... [pag·ad] /pagad/ carabao, [kuj·is] /koyis/ pig, [pal·ak] /parek/ sugar cane wine' -- presupposes final stress in such disyllables. Fn. 5 (p. 60) cites Yamada 1965 'Phonology of Itbayaten', Philippine Journal of Science 94(3): 373-393, and Tsuchida 1968 'Sketch of Itbayaten Grammar' (dittoed, New Haven) for further information.

sources.citation: Yamada, Yukihiro. 2002. Itbayat-English Dictionary (ELPR Publications Series A3-006). Osaka: Endangered Languages of the Pacific Rim, Osaka Gakuin University. iv+314 pp.
sources.note: Introduction 2.1.1 Phonemics (pp. 6-7) gives the phoneme inventory with V/VV (tokod vs tookod) and C/CC (makoto vs makkoto) contrasts and notes that a medial intervocalic consonant in disyllables is phonetically longer; nothing on stress placement. Intro 2.2.20 Suprafix (p. 18): 'It is the stress expressing the superlative degree.' maavij iya (positive) / mavyavij iya (comparative) / máavij iya (superlative) -- stress shifted onto the initial (long) syllable marks the superlative.
